Kernel `ball_less_equal_1` · **UNVERIFIED** · [all operations](index.md) · [how to read this page](reading.md)

**UNVERIFIED: no proof is checked.** The statement below is a target: Rocq has not checked a proof of it. No public operation calls it yet ([What holds today](../getting-started/guarantees.md#proved-and-unverified)).

## What it computes

The three-valued answer to whether $x \le y$ for every $x \in X, y \in Y$, $X$ and $Y$ not being empty, $X$ the ball of center $c_x$ and radius $r_x$ and $Y$ the ball of center $c_y$ and radius $r_y$: *yes* only if it holds for every choice of members, *no* only if it fails for every choice, otherwise *unknown*, both masks false:

$$\mathit{yes} \implies X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } x \le y \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y, \qquad \mathit{no} \implies X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \lnot(x \le y) \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y.$$

## C++

**Not yet called by the public headers.** No public operation computes this kernel yet.

## Requires

- $X$, of center $c_x$ and radius $r_x$, is a canonical ball: a finite ball (finite center, finite radius $\ge 0$), the whole line (center 0, radius $+\infty$), or the empty set (every limb a NaN).
- $Y$, of center $c_y$ and radius $r_y$, is a canonical ball: a finite ball (finite center, finite radius $\ge 0$), the whole line (center 0, radius $+\infty$), or the empty set (every limb a NaN).

## Target (not proved)

For operands that satisfy the requirements, finite, infinite or NaN:

- $\mathit{yes}$ is true only if $X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } x \le y \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y$; $\mathit{no}$ only if $X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \lnot(x \le y) \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y$; never both. Both false is the answer *unknown*.
- An empty operand gives *unknown*, and so does the whole line.
- When an operand is the empty set or the whole line, the answer is exact: each mask is true exactly when its relation holds.
- When every operand is finite (a finite ball) and $\lvert r_x + r_y\rvert \le \Omega$, the answer is exact as well.

Stated for every binary format with a precision of at least 2 bits, rounding to nearest with ties to even and with gradual underflow, in the IEEE model, with signed zeros, infinities, NaN and overflow. Both limb types qualify: `double` has 53 bits, `float` has 24 bits.

## Status

**UNVERIFIED.** No proof of the statement is checked. The [Proofs](../proofs/index.md#what-is-proved-and-in-which-model) page says which statements of the IEEE model are proved against statements written by hand; this page gives the status that `gen/claims.json` gives.

## Source

**Algorithm:** the sum of the radii and the differences of the centers as exact pairs, compared (Milestone 2 listing). **License:** algorithm and proof: MIT.

## Listing

From [`gen/kernels/ball_less_equal_1.kernel`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/gen/kernels/ball_less_equal_1.kernel), the description the C++ and the formal model (`proofs/gen/IeeeModel.v`) are generated from. Each line is one operation of `T`; one that rounds rounds to nearest, and `prod(a, b)` is $\mathrm{RN}(ab)$, written as a fused multiply-add with a zero addend ([the kernel IR](../developer/architecture.md#the-kernel-ir)).
It calls [`two_sum_ord`](two_sum_ord.md), [`le_2_2`](le_2_2.md), [`lt_2_2`](lt_2_2.md).

```
# The three-valued X <= Y of balls with one-limb centers (milestone2.md, "One enclosure interface",
# "Comparisons"): yes when every member of X is at most every member of Y, r_x + r_y <= c_y - c_x,
# by le_2_2 on the exact pairs and a test that the sum of the radii is finite; no when every member
# of X is above every member of Y, r_x + r_y < c_x - c_y, by lt_2_2. Both false for an empty operand
# and for the whole line. Exact when r_x + r_y <= Omega (and also, not claimed, when the difference
# of the centers does not overflow).

(s0, s1) = two_sum_ord(rx, ry)
ncx      = neg(cx)
(d0, d1) = two_sum_ord(cy, ncx)
ncy      = neg(cy)
(g0, g1) = two_sum_ord(cx, ncy)
a        = le_2_2(s0, s1, d0, d1)
sa       = abs(s0)
fs       = lt(sa, const inf)
yes      = and(a, fs)
no       = lt_2_2(s0, s1, g0, g1)
```
